agent_notes: Hebrew verse 1 is the superscription, which the KJV leaves as verse 0 and runs into its verse 1. The five English versions agree on the shape but not on 'aiyelet hashachar': KJV and ASV transliterate it, YLT translates 'The Hind of the Morning'. I translate it and keep the tune-title reading as the main one; the commentaries (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) offer an instrument, a tune, the morning star, and Esther or Israel in exile, and I list them rather than choose.

STEPBible reads 'meracham' under hashlakhti as 'from the womb'; it is the same as the line's parallel 'from the belly of my mother'. 'hushlakhti' is Hophal (passive) of 'to throw', which I render 'I was thrown'. KJV's 'cast' is accurate; BBE 'in your hands' softens it.

agent_notes: yechidati: lit. 'my only one'. All five English versions soften it ('darling', 'life', 'only one'). Commentators in the packet read it as the soul that is one and unique (Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion). I kept 'my only one' in the literal layer and 'my one life' in the dramatic.

The shift from the imperative 'save me' to the perfect 'you have answered me' is the hinge of the psalm. Hebrew has no change of tense marker here; I kept a plain perfect in the literal layer. KJV 'unicorns' is a mistranslation of re'emim (wild oxen, aurochs) via the Greek monokeros. YLT 'high places' reads a different vocalisation (ramim) and is not followed. Radak and Meiri read 'anitani as a prophetic perfect, 'answer me'; I did not adopt this.

agent_notes: Reviewer request: the earlier English said 'the nations slain by Israel'. Radak (the second reading he gives, in his father's name) says the 'descenders to dust' are those who killed Israel, who are in Gehenna, and God will not give life to any of them (citing Joel 4:21 and Isaiah 60:17). The commentary now gives the killers, not the slain, attributed to Radak. The Hebrew itself names no nation and no Israel, so the literal and dramatic layers keep the text's own words.

The verse is a famous crux and the five English versions split. KJV, ASV and Webster read the first clause as future ('shall eat and worship'); YLT keeps the Hebrew perfect ('have eaten'). BBE turns the last clause into 'has not enough for the life of his soul'. The last clause, 'ונפשו לא חיה', has a third-person singular verb with a 'his' that has no antecedent in the plural clause before it; I kept 'his' and 'he' literally. I did not adopt any emendation of the consonants.

agent_notes: Corrected after review: citations are now attributed as the packet gives them. Ibn Ezra quotes Ps 37:5 ('גול על ה' דרכך'); Radak and Meiri compare 1 Sam 21:7 (לחם חם) and Prov 10:29 for the adjectival form. I dropped my earlier Proverbs 16:3 parallel.

The form גֹּל is ambiguous: an imperative 'Roll!' (the mockers' sarcasm), a noun/adjective 'one who rolls' (Ibn Ezra, Radak), or an infinitive 'to roll' (Rashi, Meiri's second reading). The dramatic layer takes the imperative, as the Hebrew's following jussives ('let him rescue') fit a mocking quotation; KJV and Webster's past tense 'He trusted' follows the adjectival/infinitive readings and is a harmonization.
